The excited state $\chi_2$ is sufficiently long-lived to survive to the present, with its relic fraction determined by the dark-sector conversion process $\chi_2\chi_2\leftrightarrow\chi_1\chi_1$. We find that this fraction depends strongly on the Lorentz structure of the DM--ALP interaction. Scalar transition couplings lead to nonperturbative conversion rates with a pronounced resonant structure, yielding a final excited-state fraction that varies nonmonotonically with the mediator mass, from $f_2\sim10^{-4}$ to approximately $1/2$ over the parameter range studied. The relative importance of endothermic and exothermic scattering is therefore parameter dependent. By contrast, pseudoscalar transition couplings preserve $f_2\simeq1/2$, yielding recoil spectra dominated by exothermic $\chi_2 N\to\chi_1 N$ down-scattering for the benchmarks considered. Benchmark spectra in all four scenarios can peak near the observed recoil energy of $250\,\mathrm{keV}$. Our results demonstrate that the dominant direction of inelastic scattering in direct detection can be dynamically selected by the early-Universe evolution of the dark sector. With additional data, annual modulation measurements could distinguish these scenarios. We further show that the ALP portal can be directly probed at colliders.

arxiv.org/abs/2609.38316.title: Constraints on Complex Electroweak WIMPs from Solar Capture
arxiv.org/abs/2609.38316.excerpt:
arXiv:2609.38316v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: One of the most convincing realizations of particle dark matter is provided by models based on electroweak multiplets. The lightest neutral state of such a multiplet can be a stable Majorana fermion or a real scalar, and its phenomenology is governed by two parameters: the dark matter mass and the mass splitting $\{m_\chi,\delta\}$. The sub-MeV range for $\delta$ is particularly important as it allows for a large inelastic scattering cross section. In this paper, we analyze solar capture, energy loss, and annihilation of scalar and fermionic electroweak multiplet dark matter, generalizing earlier results for the Higgsino to other representations. We find that, while the case of a doublet is somewhat special, higher representations behave in a self-similar way. For the higher multiplets, IceCube results constrain the splitting to $\delta \gtrsim 350$ keV for all dark matter masses up to $100$ TeV. Assuming thermal freeze-out and a Standard Halo Model velocity distribution, this rules out most models of electroweak dark matter as a possible origin of the single high-recoil event reported by the LZ collaboration. We also show that a high-velocity tail in the dark matter distribution, such as that induced by the Large Magellanic Cloud, raises the splitting preferred by the LZ event above the solar bounds for many of the multiplets.

arxiv.org/abs/2610.41082.title: Two-Fluid Radial Stability of Dark-Matter-Admixed Compact Objects: Dark Compact Planets, Dark White Dwarfs, Dark Neutron Stars, and Dark Oysters
arxiv.org/abs/2610.41082.excerpt:
arXiv:2610.41082v2 Announce Type: replace-cross 
Abstract: We investigate the equilibrium structure and stability against radial oscillations of a variety of two-fluid compact objects containing ordinary baryonic matter admixed with cold dark matter coupled through the background spacetime. For the ordinary fluid, we employ a QCD equation of state compatible with chiral effective field theory at nuclear densities (supplemented by the BPS and Negele-Vautherin models at extremely low densities) and with perturbative QCD in the high-density regime while also satisfying also current astrophysical data. For the dark fluid, we assume self-interacting fermionic matter with particle masses of $m_f=$ 2, 5, 10, and 100 GeV and two self-interaction strengths of $y=0.1$ and $10^3$. By scanning a large range of central pressures for both fluids, we identify the presence of dark compact planets, dark white dwarfs, dark neutron stars and the so-called dark oysters. Importantly, these objects are not only in two-fluid hydrostatic equilibrium, but they are also stable against two-fluid radial oscillations. We find that the relative representation of each class in the radially stable sample is strongly sensitive to the combinations of $m_f$ and $y$, with some combinations entirely suppressing some of these object classes within the sampled domain while favoring others. In addition to these classes, strong self-repulsion supports stable, dark-matter-dominated branches with compact ordinary-matter cores and extended dark halos, approaching the self-interacting fermion-star limit. Finally, we calculate the gravitational redshift at the ordinary-matter surface, $z_{\rm OM}$, including the contribution of extended dark-matter halos for which we found radially stable configurations with $z_{\rm OM}>2$.

phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists-wild-he.excerpt: Humans have left their mark on virtually every place on the planet, from the deep sea to the peaks of the highest mountains. But a few very remote atolls in the Pacific Ocean may be exceptions. A new Frontiers in Marine Science study has found two coral atolls, Bikar and Bokak, located on the territory of the Marshall Islands, to be some of the most intact ecosystems remaining in the region and perhaps the world.

phys.org/news/2026-11-iberian-season-lar.title: Record-breaking 2025 Iberian fire season was three times larger due to climate change
phys.org/news/2026-11-iberian-season-lar.excerpt: The latest global State of Wildfires report, co-led by the University of East Anglia, shows that the extreme fire-prone weather experienced across Spain and Portugal in 2025 was three times more likely due to human-caused climate change, and the area burned was three times larger. The paper is published in Earth System Science Data.

phys.org/news/2026-11-humility-social-we.title: Living with humility took on social weight in the late Middle Ages, historian argues
phys.org/news/2026-11-humility-social-we.excerpt: We're deep in the Middle Ages. In the mind's eye, monks stagger past, flagellating themselves to cleanse their sins and demonstrate their humility before God and creation. This was a time when humility—humilitas—was considered one of the fundamental virtues of Christian life.

phys.org/news/2026-11-important-tropical.title: More important than tropical cyclones: Scientists finally track the hidden weather systems behind most tropical rainfall
phys.org/news/2026-11-important-tropical.excerpt: For the first time, researchers in Australia have identified and tracked the weather systems that are collectively more important to rainfall across the tropics than tropical cyclones. The work, published in the journal Weather and Climate Dynamics, has advanced a new way to investigate how tropical rain may change as the Earth warms up.

phys.org/news/2026-11-pipes-status-18th-.title: How pipes became status symbols in 18th-century Sweden
phys.org/news/2026-11-pipes-status-18th-.excerpt: In the 18th century, a clay tobacco pipe could reveal more than you might think. Its length, quality and condition, as well as the way it was used, could signal social status. In a new doctoral thesis, Lund University archaeologist Robert Bergman Carter shows how smokeways at the time served as clear markers of status.

phys.org/news/2026-11-loyal-donors-advic.title: Why holding on to loyal donors is not the right advice for every nonprofit
phys.org/news/2026-11-loyal-donors-advic.excerpt: As humanitarian funding shrinks, conventional fundraising wisdom says to hold on to loyal donors. But new research shows that the value of a donor depends on how a nonprofit is set up. For many organizations, winning new donors matters more than keeping loyal ones.

phys.org/news/2026-11-similar-cloud-clim.title: Why similar changes in cloud cover can have different climate effects
phys.org/news/2026-11-similar-cloud-clim.excerpt: Marine low clouds over the world's eastern subtropical oceans strongly influence Earth's temperature by reflecting sunlight back to space. How these clouds change as the planet warms is one of the biggest uncertainties in predicting the severity of future warming.

phys.org/news/2026-11-deep-sea-mollusk-h.title: Deep-sea mollusk houses bacteria in tiny 'dragon balls,' revealing a new symbiotic structure
phys.org/news/2026-11-deep-sea-mollusk-h.excerpt: Researchers at The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (HKUST) have discovered a previously unknown specialized organelle structure in a deep-sea mollusk living at cold seeps in the South China Sea. Dedicated to maintaining bacterial symbiosis, this newly identified survival mechanism provides new insights into how deep-sea organisms adapt to nearly oxygen-free environments and opens new directions for research on chemosymbiosis, organelle evolution and deep-sea ecosystems.

phys.org/news/2026-11-method-dna-epigene.title: New method maps DNA folding and epigenetic marks in single cells
phys.org/news/2026-11-method-dna-epigene.excerpt: A new experimental procedure developed by researchers at Yale School of Medicine could help scientists better understand how DNA structure influences disease and development.

phys.org/news/2026-11-drylands-microbes-.title: When rain finally does come to drylands, only some microbes in the soil 'awaken'
phys.org/news/2026-11-drylands-microbes-.excerpt: In arid regions, the microbes that power threatened dryland soil ecosystems called biological soil crusts stay dormant over long periods, only "awakening" when they sense moisture from infrequent rainfall. Now, a team led by researchers at Penn State—driven by projections that those biocrusts will decline by as much as 40% in the next 45 years—found that when a dryland soil does get wet, most of the microbes in the biocrust stay inactive. It's a discovery that will inform ongoing efforts to conserve and restore biocrusts, according to the researchers.

phys.org/news/2026-11-biologists-reveal-.title: Biologists reveal chlorophyll-building enzyme's structure for first time and clarify its mechanism
phys.org/news/2026-11-biologists-reveal-.excerpt: Plants are green because of a pigment that is key to photosynthesis: chlorophyll. In its production, the enzyme chlorophyll synthase plays an important role. As part of an international collaboration, researchers from Osnabrück University, the Center Algatech in Třeboň and the University of Sheffield have now succeeded in deciphering the structure of this enzyme and gaining valuable insights into its mechanism. The findings are published in the journal Nature Chemical Biology.

phys.org/news/2026-11-biodegradable-lact.title: Biodegradable bubble moves away from lactic acid without a motor—a step toward artificial cells
phys.org/news/2026-11-biodegradable-lact.excerpt: A tiny biodegradable bubble can move away from a chemical on its own, without a motor. Living cells need complex molecular machinery to do this. This discovery by researchers led by chemist Daniela Wilson at Radboud University, together with colleagues at Durham University, is a step toward artificial cells with lifelike behavior and could, in the long term, provide an interesting approach for self-steering particles in targeted drug delivery.

phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists-extinct.title: Scientists challenge the dream of bringing extinct species back to life
phys.org/news/2026-11-scientists-extinct.excerpt: Could extinction itself become a thing of the past? Advances in biotechnology, including ancient DNA sequencing, genome analysis and gene editing, have led some to believe that it may be possible to bring extinct species back to life.

phys.org/news/2026-11-chip-cells-electri.title: Chip identifies cells by their electrical signature, then separates them with a precisely aimed sound wave
phys.org/news/2026-11-chip-cells-electri.excerpt: In biomedicine, sorting cells accurately without damaging them remains a persistent problem. Current methods, like fluorescence-activated cell sorting, rely on labeling the cells extrinsically, which can stress the cells, alter their behavior and even interfere with the assay. A collaborative study between researchers in Singapore and China has now developed a noninvasive, label-free method to sort cells.

phys.org/news/2026-11-remedy-proactive-a.title: From remedy to prevention: Researchers call for proactive approach to protect the human right to water
phys.org/news/2026-11-remedy-proactive-a.excerpt: More than 2 billion people, or approximately one-quarter of the world's population, lack access to safe water, sanitation and hygiene, according to the United Nations Children's Fund. Today, 16 years after the U.N. General Assembly recognized this access as a fundamental human right, its legal protection is well established, but the reality on the ground lags behind.

phys.org/news/2026-11-clay-figurines-pre.title: Symbolic clay figurines change our understanding of the prehistoric Middle East
phys.org/news/2026-11-clay-figurines-pre.excerpt: Newly discovered artifacts are evidence of the earliest known example of a tradition of making clay figurines in the Middle East—and challenge long-held beliefs about when and how clay began to be used for symbolic purposes in the region, according to a study published in PLOS One by Laurent Davin from The Hebrew University of Jerusalem, Israel, and colleagues.

phys.org/news/2026-11-monkey-foot-palm-d.title: Monkey foot and palm prints differ between individuals, as they do in humans
phys.org/news/2026-11-monkey-foot-palm-d.excerpt: In three species of monkey, the complex pattern of ridges on the feet and palms varies between individuals, similar to human fingerprints, according to a study published in the open-access journal PLOS One by Juliana Vieira Flores Sales at Universidade de Brasília and colleagues.

phys.org/news/2026-11-statistics-common-.title: Misunderstandings about statistics common even among experienced researchers
phys.org/news/2026-11-statistics-common-.excerpt: Even researchers and people with extensive training in statistics often find it difficult to interpret statistical results correctly. This is shown by a new systematic review carried out by Uppsala University and others, in which researchers have analyzed 55 studies involving over 15,000 participants. The work is published in PLOS One.

phys.org/news/2026-11-spain-massive-ston.title: Spain's massive stone tombs reveal collective burials continued well into Bronze Age
phys.org/news/2026-11-spain-massive-ston.excerpt: Iberian people continued using, and possibly building, massive necropolises well into the Bronze Age, according to a study published in PLOS One by Eduardo Vijande-Vila of the University of Cádiz, Spain, and colleagues.

phys.org/news/2026-11-frozen-sperm-enabl.title: Frozen sperm enables embryo development in endangered Japanese bird for first time—but chick fails to hatch
phys.org/news/2026-11-frozen-sperm-enabl.excerpt: The Okinawa rail (Hypotaenidia okinawae) is an endangered flightless bird endemic to the Yanbaru forest region of Okinawa Island in Japan. The bird has only recently begun recovering its numbers after introduced predators, such as the mongoose, and traffic accidents reduced its population to as low as 820 individuals.

phys.org/news/2026-11-overheating-cattle.title: Overheating cattle: More and more dangerous heat is coming for northern Australia's herds
phys.org/news/2026-11-overheating-cattle.excerpt: The Sunday roast and the backyard barbecue have long been Australian rituals. The country is one of the world's biggest consumers of red meat. The average Australian ate about 22 kilograms (49 pounds) of beef in 2024.

phys.org/news/2026-11-excess-reliance-ai.title: Excess reliance on AI could harm independent thinking in humanities education
phys.org/news/2026-11-excess-reliance-ai.excerpt: The increasing use of content generated using artificial intelligence (AI) tools in university humanities classrooms is challenging what we think of as traditional academic integrity, intellectual responsibility and the authority of teachers, according to research in the International Journal of Innovation and Sustainable Development.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-dna-reveal.title: Ancient DNA reveals rare genetic condition behind a 1,600-year-old infant's single eye socket
phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-dna-reveal.excerpt: Cyclopia is the most severe form of a rare birth condition in which the developing brain fails to divide into two separate halves. This can also affect facial development, sometimes leaving the baby with a single eye socket in the center of the forehead and severe facial abnormalities. Most babies born with this condition either die before or soon after birth. It is so rare that it occurs in roughly 1 in 100,000 births, so finding physical evidence of it from modern times is difficult, let alone from historical ones.

phys.org/news/2026-11-defense-photosynth.title: A double defense protects photosynthesis from extreme heat
phys.org/news/2026-11-defense-photosynth.excerpt: Photosynthesis is fundamental to life on Earth, allowing plants and microalgae to convert sunlight and carbon dioxide into organic compounds. However, this essential process is highly vulnerable to heat. As global temperatures rise and heat waves become more frequent, declining photosynthetic efficiency threatens agricultural productivity and the large-scale cultivation of microalgae for biofuels and other valuable products.

phys.org/news/2026-11-3d-protein-complex.title: 3D protein complex model sheds light on barley grain dormancy
phys.org/news/2026-11-3d-protein-complex.excerpt: Researchers from Adelaide University and Plant Synthetic Biology Australia have uncovered new insights into the molecular machinery controlling the dormancy-to-germination transition in barley, potentially paving the way for improved crop varieties and better outcomes for farmers, maltsters and brewers.

phys.org/news/2026-11-account-role-negle.title: Taking into account the role of neglected farmer groups in recharging groundwater
phys.org/news/2026-11-account-role-negle.excerpt: A new study by researchers at the Indo-French Cell for Water Sciences (IFCWS), Indian Institute of Science (IISc), introduces a new framework for water budgeting in agricultural regions that includes farmers' social categories that are usually neglected. The work is published in the Journal of Hydrology.

phys.org/news/2026-11-centaurus-spotligh.title: Centaurus A in the spotlight: Plasma simulations reproduce black hole jets' mysterious bright edges
phys.org/news/2026-11-centaurus-spotligh.excerpt: Around 12 million light-years away, the supermassive black hole of the galaxy Centaurus A is hurling two enormous plasma jets into space at nearly the speed of light. These so-called jets are brighter at their edges than at their center. The reason for this was previously unclear but has now been explained by a team from the Chair of Astronomy at the University of Würzburg. The research is published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

livescience.com/archaeology/2-200-year-o.title: 2,200-year-old gold bear figurine and surprising number of bones found in massive burial mound in Kazakhstan
livescience.com/archaeology/2-200-year-o.excerpt: Archaeologists have found a 2,200-year-old golden bear in an Iron Age burial in Kazakhstan that may have held seven people.

livescience.com/planet-earth/geology/the.title: The Grand Canyon is missing over a billion years of rocks. Now scientists know why.
livescience.com/planet-earth/geology/the.excerpt: The mission 1.2 billion years of geological history at the Grand Canyon finally has an explanation.

livescience.com/physics-mathematics/part.excerpt: A proposed tabletop quantum sensor could match the precision of the best satellite measurements of frame dragging, a subtle effect predicted by Einstein's general relativity.

livescience.com/chemistry/floridas-dark-.excerpt: Scientists have discovered that a known mushroom, Galerina indica , contains both psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins.

statnews.com/2026/11/11/all-of-us-study-.excerpt: A study of nearly 100,000 diverse Americans identified thousands of new variants in genes that influence our responses to prescription drugs

statnews.com/2026/11/11/obesity-diagnosi.title: STAT+: BMI alternative would flip obesity diagnosis for millions, study finds
statnews.com/2026/11/11/obesity-diagnosi.excerpt: A newly proposed way of identifying obesity could flip the diagnoses of millions of people. Proponents argue it could lead to more precise care.

space.com/astronomy/mars/nasa-kick-start.title: NASA kick-starts a fresh push to bring Mars samples home
space.com/astronomy/mars/nasa-kick-start.excerpt: NASA is kickstarting a new initiative for Mars Sample Return (MSR), called the Perseverance Sample Retrieval Architecture.

space.com/astronomy/we-cant-see-fast-rad.title: We can't see Fast Radio Bursts but we can now hear them thanks to a Finnish Cathedral
space.com/astronomy/we-cant-see-fast-rad.excerpt: Fast radio bursts are invisible, but a composer has turned thousands of them into sound at a Finnish cathedral, where a choir will sing along on Nov. 21.

space.com/space-exploration/on-this-day-.title: On this day in space! Nov. 11, 1966: NASA launches Gemini 12 mission with astronaut icons Buzz Aldrin and Jim Lovell aboard
space.com/space-exploration/on-this-day-.excerpt: On Nov. 11, 1966, the Gemini 12 mission launched an astronaut crew into orbit and set the stage for NASA's Apollo program. Here's why it mattered.

space.com/astronomy/exoplanets/andy-weir.excerpt: How would the crew of the Wild Blue Yonder fare on a real exoplanet?

space.com/astronomy/comets/did-comets-br.title: Did comets bring building blocks of life to Earth? Scientists aren't so sure anymore
space.com/astronomy/comets/did-comets-br.excerpt: For over a century astronomers have speculated that comets could have delivered organic molecules necessary for life to Earth, but new modeling shows these molecules wouldn't have survived impact.

space.com/space-exploration/launches-spa.title: 'There's tremendous demand': Rocket Lab raises price of Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million
space.com/space-exploration/launches-spa.excerpt: Rocket Lab has raised the launch cost of its next-gen Neutron rocket by more than 25%, an increase that reflects high demand amid a looming liftoff bottleneck.

astronomy.com/observing/zwo-introduces-t.title: ZWO introduces the Seestar S30 Plus
astronomy.com/observing/zwo-introduces-t.excerpt: ZWO has added a new entry point to its smart telescope lineup. The Seestar S30 Plus went on sale Nov. 10 for $499 — $474 for a limited time — undercutting the S30 Pro by $200 and making it the cheapest Seestar available. “Many people are interested in astrophotography but hesitate when they see the Continue reading "ZWO introduces the Seestar S30 Plus" The post ZWO introduces the Seestar S30 Plus appeared first on Astronomy Magazine .

universetoday.com/articles/the-ice-giant.title: The Ice Giants' Magnetic Fields are Very Strange Compared to Earth's
universetoday.com/articles/the-ice-giant.excerpt: Uranus and Neptune, the Solar System's ice giants, have interiors unlike the other planets. As a result, they also have magnetic fields unlike the others. They're messy and tilted, and Voyager 2, the only spacecraft to even flyby them, showed us how messy they are. New research uses models to try to understand what's going on with the pair of planets and their weird fields, and found that it's likely they change on very short timescales. They could already be much different than when Voyager 2 visited in the late 1980s.

universetoday.com/articles/asteroid-mini.title: Asteroid Mining Will Crash the Platinum Market, But That’s Good News for Earth
universetoday.com/articles/asteroid-mini.excerpt: Science fiction authors have been dreaming of robotic spacecraft harvesting fortunes from asteroids for decades. Humanity is slowly getting closer to that reality. But if you ask asteroid mining skeptics, they will usually ask one specific question - what happens to the prices of all those rare materials once someone actually brings them back? A pair of system dynamicists from MIT directly tackled that question with a new paper titled Will AstroForge Collapse the PGM Market?

universetoday.com/articles/the-chandra-x.title: The Chandra X-Ray Observatory Unmasks a Supernova Impostor
universetoday.com/articles/the-chandra-x.excerpt: Some stars, called Luminous Blue Variables, can be confused with supernovae explosions. They exhibit similar outbursts, but unlike supernovae, which explode once and then are gone forever, these stars have periodic outbursts. New research found that one of these 'supernova impostors' is in a binary relationship with a black hole or a neutron star, and that explains its periodic outbursts.

newscientist.com/article/2598571-some-pf.title: Some PFAS chemicals are declining in English rivers but others are appearing
newscientist.com/article/2598571-some-pf.excerpt: The levels of two globally restricted "forever chemicals" linked to health issues are showing a strong downwards trend in English rivers, but their understudied replacements are starting to fill the gap

phys.org/news/2026-11-romania-kazakhstan.title: From Romania to Kazakhstan, summer droughts linked to less winter ice in two rapidly warming seas
phys.org/news/2026-11-romania-kazakhstan.excerpt: This summer, with its scarce rainfall and repeated heat waves, witnessed one of the most severe droughts in Europe since 1540. The resulting wildfires across western Europe received considerable media attention, but eastern Europe was also heavily hit, worsening the humanitarian crisis caused by the war in Ukraine. Simulations have shown that such droughts are bound to become more frequent and severe in the future due to man-made global warming.

phys.org/news/2026-11-war-world-years.ht.title: How war has connected the world for 500 years
phys.org/news/2026-11-war-world-years.ht.excerpt: With wars raging in Ukraine and across the Middle East, commentators increasingly ask whether we're sliding toward a third world war. But what makes a war "global"?

phys.org/news/2026-11-indonesia-million-.title: Indonesia fires burned through nearly 2.9 million hectares: Monitor
phys.org/news/2026-11-indonesia-million-.excerpt: Fires in Indonesia driven partly by a strong El Niño have burned through 2.88 million hectares (7.1 million acres) so far in 2026, a monitor analyzing satellite imagery told AFP on Wednesday.

phys.org/news/2026-11-england-young-work.title: Only half of England's young workers outside higher education secure permanent contracts, down from 81%
phys.org/news/2026-11-england-young-work.excerpt: The study of young people in England found that among those who did not progress to higher education, only 16% secured apprenticeships and just 23% had secured stable work by ages 19–20. Of those in work, only half had a permanent contract, down from 81% in a similar study six years ago.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-liner-larges.title: Retired ocean liner to become largest artificial reef in the world
phys.org/news/2026-11-ocean-liner-larges.excerpt: Bigger than the RMS Titanic and faster than the RMS Queen Mary, the SS United States was a nautical wonder during the mid-20th century—the nation's premier luxury ocean liner that once ferried presidents and Hollywood elite across the Atlantic in opulence.

phys.org/news/2026-11-microplastics-wild.title: Microplastics found in wild mammals' blood more than 40 miles from human infrastructure
phys.org/news/2026-11-microplastics-wild.excerpt: Animals, like humans, are taking up increasing amounts of tiny plastic particles. Such microplastics are demonstrably hazardous to many species under experimental conditions, and it is suspected that they may also pose a threat to animals in the wild. While data about microplastic concentrations in the terrestrial environment exist, it has not yet been clear if higher exposure also translates into higher microplastic accumulation in individual animals. A new paper published in Nature now confirms this link.

phys.org/news/2026-11-genetic-landscape-.title: New study maps the genetic landscape of bovine TB across Wales
phys.org/news/2026-11-genetic-landscape-.excerpt: Bovine tuberculosis is evolving in different ways across different regions in Wales, according to the most detailed analysis of the bacterium conducted to date. One of the most significant animal health challenges facing Wales, bovine TB affects cattle health and farm businesses and places considerable emotional, social and financial pressures on farming communities.

phys.org/news/2026-11-parasites-fungus-i.title: Even parasites have parasites: Fungus infects powdery mildew
phys.org/news/2026-11-parasites-fungus-i.excerpt: In the fungal kingdom, no one is safe from parasites—not even other parasites. A new study from North Carolina State University finds that Ampelomyces, an intracellular fungus that infects the plant disease powdery mildew, is far more common than previously known. By screening museum samples of powdery mildews up to about 150 years old, researchers discovered that not only is Ampelomyces quite common, but many specimens labeled as Ampelomyces are misidentified.

phys.org/news/2026-11-independent-techni.title: Independent technique validates landmark M87* image
phys.org/news/2026-11-independent-techni.excerpt: The 2019 Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) image was the work of hundreds of scientists and captured the first direct view of a black hole's shadow—becoming one of the most recognized scientific images of the modern era. A team of four from CSIRO, Australia's national science agency, has developed a powerful new imaging technique that validated the landmark 2019 image of the black hole at the center of galaxy M87.

phys.org/news/2026-11-hidden-technology-.title: Clean water, hidden risks: New technology reveals neurotoxicity missed by conventional water quality monitoring
phys.org/news/2026-11-hidden-technology-.excerpt: A photograph of an orchestra can tell you whether the musicians are on stage and their instruments are intact. But it cannot tell you whether they are playing in harmony. Even when every musician is present, a subtle loss of coordination can change the entire performance.

phys.org/news/2026-11-fluorescent-probes.title: Fluorescent probes reveal fluid-like barriers inside nuclear pores of living human cells
phys.org/news/2026-11-fluorescent-probes.excerpt: Our genetic material is hidden inside the nucleus of our cells, well protected by a double membrane. All molecules wishing to pass through must thread their way through one of several thousand nuclear pores. The scaffold structure of these pores is well known. However, exactly how transport takes place within them has been the subject of much debate. Researchers at Johannes Gutenberg University Mainz (JGU), the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics (MPI-BP) in Frankfurt am Main and Wuhan University in China have now shed light on the matter.

phys.org/news/2026-11-superconducting-vo.title: Superconducting vortices provide experimental evidence that clogging is a phase transition
phys.org/news/2026-11-superconducting-vo.excerpt: Clogging is a phenomenon in which moving particles get stuck, slowing or blocking the flow, but how this transition occurs has remained experimentally unproven. Researchers from Science Tokyo studied superconducting vortices to demonstrate that clogging is a nonequilibrium phase transition. Using a two-step measurement protocol, they distinguished clogging from conventional pinning and revealed that both transitions share a critical point, offering new insights into predicting and controlling clogging across diverse systems.

phys.org/news/2026-11-lurks-newfoundland.title: What lurks 'Below' Newfoundland waters? A marine biologist explains the science behind the show
phys.org/news/2026-11-lurks-newfoundland.excerpt: When I learned that Netflix planned to film the miniseries Below, about a sea monster terrorizing a Newfoundland outport, I thought to myself: "THIS I've gotta see!"

phys.org/news/2026-11-looping-dna-nectar.title: Looping DNA may help flowers grow nectar-producing organs
phys.org/news/2026-11-looping-dna-nectar.excerpt: Nectaries are specialized floral tissues that secrete nectar to attract pollinators. Although the protein CRABS CLAW (CRC) is established as essential for nectary formation, the exact molecular mechanisms governing how it drives organ growth and secretion have remained unknown.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261110.title: A massive new simulation reveals how the universe emerged from darkness

Phytoplankton support zooplankton, which in turn transfer energy to fish and other animals. Changes in phytoplankton communities can therefore lead to cascading effects on marine food webs.

Often, it can feel uncomfortable talking about people's differences; conversations about racism reveal implicit biases and, for some, immense privilege.

phys.org/news/2026-11-advances-quantum-h.title: Research advances quantum computing that harnesses speed of light
phys.org/news/2026-11-advances-quantum-h.excerpt: Quantum computers have the potential to perform calculations more quickly than supercomputers, but they could be even faster and more energy-efficient if they were built with photons as their basic units, called qubits.

phys.org/news/2026-11-automated-space-fu.title: Automated assembly in space is the future and NOM4D is showing the way
phys.org/news/2026-11-automated-space-fu.excerpt: If we want big things in space, we'll have to build and assemble them there. Rocket fairings are not large enough to accommodate the large things we want to have in space. Not only that, but the stubborn rocket equation refuses to bend itself to our desires.

phys.org/news/2026-11-moon-wild-west-exp.title: The moon is not the Wild West: Experts call for a pause on lunar industrialization
phys.org/news/2026-11-moon-wild-west-exp.excerpt: As the major powers and the private companies go full tilt with their plans to develop infrastructure and extract resources on the moon, the questions around environmental protection, international regulation and who benefits all come into play. Vilnius University Institute of International Relations and Political Science (VU IIRPS) professor Florian Rabitz, together with Xiao-Shan Yap from Utrecht University, explores these concerns in their research article, "Don't Fly Me to the Moon: A Moratorium on Lunar Industrialization," published in the journal Global Environmental Politics.

phys.org/news/2026-11-online-networking-.title: Trusted online information may help networking skills translate into startup ambitions, survey suggests
phys.org/news/2026-11-online-networking-.excerpt: A study of almost 200 undergraduate and postgraduate students in South Korea suggests that the skills of aspiring entrepreneurs are more likely to translate into plans to start a business when supported by trustworthy digital networks and useful online resources. Details of the findings are reported in the World Review of Entrepreneurship, Management and Sustainable Development.

phys.org/news/2026-11-vision-interferome.title: Vision and interferometry improve calibration of large monolithic mirrors
phys.org/news/2026-11-vision-interferome.excerpt: In a new study published in Measurement, researchers from the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have developed a calibration method that combines machine vision with interferometry. This method separates a mirror's fixed internal offset from changes in the test path alignment.

phys.org/news/2026-11-populist-leaders-d.title: How populist leaders dismantle intelligence agencies from within: New study reveals the 'intelligence cyclone'
phys.org/news/2026-11-populist-leaders-d.excerpt: A new joint study from Ben-Gurion University of the Negev (BGU) and The Hebrew University of Jerusalem reveals how populist leaderships systematically undermine, discredit and ultimately capture intelligence agencies, transforming vital national security bodies into political echo chambers. The research, published in Contemporary Security Policy, warns that when populist politicians treat secret services as "deep state" adversaries, they disrupt objective threat analysis and leave democracies blind to catastrophic surprise attacks.

phys.org/news/2026-11-climate-consequenc.title: Climate change has different consequences for the health of women and men
phys.org/news/2026-11-climate-consequenc.excerpt: The health risks men and women are exposed to and the illnesses they develop vary widely across lifetimes and places. Yet climate policy and health services often overlook these differences.

phys.org/news/2026-11-black-rhinos-loner.title: Black rhinos are mostly loners, but not always: Why this matters for saving the species
phys.org/news/2026-11-black-rhinos-loner.excerpt: Black rhinos are notoriously aggressive, not just to humans but also to their fellow black rhinos. Aggression is so prevalent that injuries sustained after fighting with another black rhino are a common cause of death. Because of this aggression and their solitary nature, black rhino social behavior has been largely unexplored. Yet it may be key to conservation of this critically endangered African icon.

phys.org/news/2026-11-early-stock-instab.title: Early signs of stock market instability may appear in how traders place orders
phys.org/news/2026-11-early-stock-instab.excerpt: The influence of financial markets cannot be overstated, and this influence highlights the need for thorough market analysis. However, being thorough can be difficult when markets are highly complex and ever-changing, prompting the search for a suitable approach to analysis. Fortunately, the increasing availability of detailed market data, together with advances in mathematical theories, offers new opportunities to better understand market behavior.

phys.org/news/2026-11-magnetic-nanoparti.title: Magnetic nanoparticles cut adhesive curing from 24 hours to one in laboratory tests
phys.org/news/2026-11-magnetic-nanoparti.excerpt: Scientists at Nanyang Technological University, Singapore (NTU Singapore) and global automotive supplier Motherson are collaborating to develop a magnetic heating technology that could significantly reduce the time and energy needed to cure industrial coatings.

phys.org/news/2026-11-robotic-tools-hidd.title: Robotic tools help unlock the hidden microbial world of the deep sea
phys.org/news/2026-11-robotic-tools-hidd.excerpt: Scientists have developed a robotic system that can recreate the extreme conditions of the deep ocean in the laboratory, opening up access to some microorganisms for the first time.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-bioplastics.htm.title: Using AI to predict how bioplastics behave under heat
phys.org/news/2026-11-ai-bioplastics.htm.excerpt: A new ANIPH study shows how machine learning models can predict how PHB and PHBV respond to heat, helping manufacturers design formulations that are easier to process.

phys.org/news/2026-11-earth-orbital-asym.title: Earth's orbital asymmetries share recurring rhythms with El Niño, study finds
phys.org/news/2026-11-earth-orbital-asym.excerpt: Every few years, an unusual warming of surface waters across the central and eastern tropical Pacific—known as El Niño—reorganizes atmospheric circulation worldwide, bringing severe droughts to some continents and torrential rainfall to others. For decades, oceanographers and meteorologists have mapped the intricate internal machinery behind the El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO), from shifting trade winds to subsurface ocean waves.

phys.org/news/2026-11-atomic-interaction.title: Engineered atomic interactions help microwave sensor capture three times as much information
phys.org/news/2026-11-atomic-interaction.excerpt: Researchers from the Faculty of Physics at the University of Warsaw (UW) and the Center for Optical Quantum Technologies at the University of Warsaw's Center for New Technologies (CeNT UW) have developed a method for ultrasensitive microwave sensing. Using cold, strongly interacting Rydberg atoms as a microwave detector, the researchers observed that carefully engineered interactions between the atoms make the atomic state resistant to loss.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ghosts-curiosity-f.title: Not afraid of ghosts: Curiosity and fearlessness apparent in German shepherd genes
phys.org/news/2026-11-ghosts-curiosity-f.excerpt: German shepherd dogs bred for working are more curious and less neurotic than German shepherds bred for show. A new study from Uppsala University and the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences has shown that the differences are not only apparent in the dogs' behavior, but also in their genes. In previous studies, similar genes in humans have been associated with neuroticism. The research is published in the journal Animal Genetics.

phys.org/news/2026-11-global-climate-pol.title: Global climate policies continue to advance despite setbacks, research finds
phys.org/news/2026-11-global-climate-pol.excerpt: The latest findings from the Oxford Climate Policy Monitor, led by the Blavatnik School of Government and the Oxford Sustainable Law Programme, show that progress in Asia, Africa and Latin America is more than offsetting the weakening or reversal of climate policies in parts of Europe and North America.

phys.org/news/2026-11-product-agricultur.title: Product for controlling agricultural pests proves harmful to iconic banana slug
phys.org/news/2026-11-product-agricultur.excerpt: Researchers at Oregon State University say a product used to control pest slugs on farms in multiple countries is harmful to an iconic West Coast slug and that more research is needed before the product is approved for use in the United States. The work is published in the journal PLOS One.

phys.org/news/2026-11-unknowns-play-majo.title: Unknowns play a major role in mortgage foreclosure decisions
phys.org/news/2026-11-unknowns-play-majo.excerpt: When it comes to making decisions regarding mortgage foreclosures, a bank doesn't know what it doesn't know.

phys.org/news/2026-11-parrots-vibrant-fe.title: Parrots' vibrant feathers are surprisingly susceptible to bacterial attack
phys.org/news/2026-11-parrots-vibrant-fe.excerpt: Flashy birds, from peacocks to parrots, have inspired a long tradition of using animal colors to study evolution. Colorful plumage often functions as a signal—for example, to attract a mate. Alternatively, drab colors can be used for camouflage. However, color can have functions beyond signaling and camouflage. This is because pigments, the molecules embedded in feather tissues to produce a broad range of colors, can also influence other aspects of feathers, ranging from mechanical strength to thermoregulatory properties.

phys.org/news/2026-11-multiplexed-detect.title: Multiplexed detector system precisely counts more than 9,000 photons
phys.org/news/2026-11-multiplexed-detect.excerpt: Researchers have developed a new approach that can precisely count from zero to more than 9,000 individual photons. The advance opens new possibilities for studying quantum light at large scales and making precise optical measurements.

phys.org/news/2026-11-mechanism-pests.ht.title: Plant sensing mechanism guards against pests
phys.org/news/2026-11-mechanism-pests.ht.excerpt: A new study has identified a previously unknown mechanism by which plants sense insect attack and activate defense responses.

phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-climate-re.title: Ancient climate records reveal how East Asian monsoon shifted abruptly into cold and drought
phys.org/news/2026-11-ancient-climate-re.excerpt: How does climate change affect the East Asian monsoon? Researchers from Utrecht University's Faculty of Geosciences, together with colleagues at research institutes in China and Belgium, are investigating this question by looking back 250,000 years. They found that, over long timescales, the monsoon system tracks changes in incoming solar radiation caused by variations in Earth's orbit and tilt. But when radiation falls below a certain threshold, abrupt periods of extreme cold and drought occur, particularly when atmospheric CO₂ concentrations are low. The study was published in Communications Earth & Environment.

phys.org/news/2026-11-dome-overlooked-hi.title: 2021 heat dome a 'near miss' as study suggests overlooked historic heat wave could offer valuable lessons
phys.org/news/2026-11-dome-overlooked-hi.excerpt: A new study suggests that the impacts of the 2021 heat dome could have been much worse for British Columbians, despite its widespread devastation, when compared to a previously overlooked heat wave during World War II.

phys.org/news/2026-11-matterantimatter-a.title: Matter–antimatter asymmetry still provides no evidence of new physics
phys.org/news/2026-11-matterantimatter-a.excerpt: The universe's dominance by ordinary matter is compelling evidence that matter and antimatter are not perfect reflections of each other. However, known differences do not explain the scale of this imbalance, leaving open the possibility that unknown physics is responsible. A new analysis of meson decays, conducted by the LHCb collaboration, has narrowed the scope of the search for such a scenario while paving the way for more precise measurements in the future.

phys.org/news/2026-11-extreme-weather-bi.title: Extreme weather risk is scaring big corporations away from poorer countries—that hurts the companies, too
phys.org/news/2026-11-extreme-weather-bi.excerpt: When multinational companies decide where to build a factory, open a mine or establish a regional office, they have to consider whether the investment will still be profitable years into the future.

phys.org/news/2026-11-chip-based-laser-c.title: Chip-based laser cooling could ease quantum computing bottleneck
phys.org/news/2026-11-chip-based-laser-c.excerpt: Researchers at Cornell have developed a laser-cooling technique that could potentially remove a significant bottleneck in the development of larger, faster quantum computers.

phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-threatens-h.title: El Niño threatens health, too—early warnings done right can save lives
phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-threatens-h.excerpt: As communities around the world shore up their infrastructure in anticipation of one of the most powerful El Niños on record in late 2026 and early 2027, they need to think about rising health risks, too—and include them in early weather warnings.

phys.org/news/2026-11-europe-alike-alpin.title: Europe's look-alike Alpine newts turn out to be five distinct species
phys.org/news/2026-11-europe-alike-alpin.excerpt: What scientists until recently called the Alpine newt has turned out to be five different species, following genetic research by Leiden biologists. One of these species was even new to science and has now been given a name: Mesotriton similis.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261112.title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261112.excerpt: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261111.title: NASA’s Perseverance confirms a key ingredient for life hidden in ancient Mars rocks
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261111.excerpt: NASA's Perseverance rover has confirmed complex organic carbon just beneath the surface of ancient Martian rocks, raising intriguing questions about the Red Planet's potential to have supported life. The remarkable preservation of these compounds, along with similar discoveries thousands of miles away, suggests the building blocks of life may once have been widespread across Mars.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261111.title: Crows can make decisions twice as fast as humans, scientists discover
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261111.excerpt: Crows may be even smarter than we thought, and their brains are astonishingly fast. Researchers at the University of Tübingen discovered that crows can make visual decisions twice as quickly as humans and monkeys, taking just 235 milliseconds on average to identify the direction of moving dots while maintaining remarkable accuracy.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261110.title: A butterfly that fooled scientists for 200 years finally reveals its secrets
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261110.excerpt: Researchers have discovered that a familiar tropical butterfly actually belongs to three nearly identical species, including one previously unknown to science. Hidden ultraviolet wing patterns and DNA differences revealed the truth, leaving scientists puzzled about how the butterflies remain genetically separate despite living side by side.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261110.title: AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again
sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261110.excerpt: Scientists have developed an AI-powered approach that makes experimental bionic vision technology more precise, helping predict the flashes and shapes of light perceived by a blind man with a brain implant. By learning how an individual's brain responds to electrical stimulation, the technology could bring researchers closer to restoring some degree of sight to people with blindness.

sciencealert.com/hundreds-of-stone-age-r.excerpt: Missed by spelunkers, treasure hunters, and tourists alike. ScienceAlert stories are written, fact-checked, and edited by humans, never generated by AI. Don't miss a story, subscribe here.

space.com/space-exploration/launches-spa.title: Watch SpaceX attempt a historic Starship launch and double-catch landing today (Nov. 13)
space.com/space-exploration/launches-spa.excerpt: SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on an unprecedented double-catch mission today (Nov. 13), and you can watch the action live.

astronomy.com/the-sky-this-week/the-sky-.title: The Sky This Week from November 13 to 20: The Leonids peak
astronomy.com/the-sky-this-week/the-sky-.excerpt: Friday, November 20The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will be 252,040 miles (405,619 kilometers) from Earth. Already 60° high in the east by 8 P.M. local time is M33, the Pinwheel Galaxy in Triangulum. This lovely spiral glows at 6th Continue reading "The Sky This Week from November 13 to 20: The Leonids peak" The post The Sky This Week from November 13 to 20: The Leonids peak appeared first on Astronomy Magazine .

universetoday.com/articles/euclids-first.title: Euclid's First Data Release: A Stepping Stone to its 3D Map of the Sky
universetoday.com/articles/euclids-first.excerpt: The ESA's Euclid Space Telescope has released its first huge batch of data. It's all part of the telescope's mission to study dark energy and dark matter. The telescope is busy creating the largest ever 3D map of the Universe with its huge 600 megapixel camera, and new images give us some highlights.

nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03456-7.title: Chinese graduate students are now choosing to stay closer to home
nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03456-7.excerpt: Nature, Published online: 13 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03456-7 Malaysia, Hong Kong and Macau are the new hot destinations for students.

nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03516-y.title: Accept all changes
nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03516-y.excerpt: Nature, Published online: 13 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03516-y It’s the end — or is it?

nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03679-8.title: This AI ‘mechanic’ can peer inside the black box of other neural networks
nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03679-8.excerpt: Nature, Published online: 13 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03679-8 Being able to target and debug systems could improve artificial-intelligence safety and utility.

nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03716-6.title: Is the climate totally cooked? What the data say
nature.com/articles/d41586-026-03716-6.excerpt: Nature, Published online: 13 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03716-6 In the first of our new podcast series, a Nature reporter looks for reasons for hope in the face of overwhelming climate anxiety.

newscientist.com/article/2594152-think-y.title: Think you know science? Try our quiz set by Nobel laureates
newscientist.com/article/2594152-think-y.excerpt: Test your knowledge of Nobel-prizewinning discoveries in microbiology, genomics and cosmology with questions set by the laureates themselves: Barry Marshall, Jennifer Doudna and Saul Perlmutter

newscientist.com/article/2598587-why-we-.title: Why we buy: 5 thinking errors companies exploit to make you shop
newscientist.com/article/2598587-why-we-.excerpt: As we near Black Friday, columnist David Robson explores the psychology behind our impulse to buy things – and how marketers take advantage of our brains to push us to purchase

phys.org/news/2026-11-wheatai-wheat-farm.title: WheatAI could speed wheat breeding and help farmers assess crops
phys.org/news/2026-11-wheatai-wheat-farm.excerpt: Wheat researchers at South Dakota State University are perfecting an AI-powered web application designed to speed the work of wheat breeders and equip farmers with a more accurate tool for making decisions.

phys.org/news/2026-11-fish-pregnancy-une.title: Fish prove every pregnancy is a battle: Unexpected evidence for the food fight between mothers and babies
phys.org/news/2026-11-fish-pregnancy-une.excerpt: Left to their own devices, babies in the womb would suck their mothers dry. A developing baby benefits from taking as many essential nutrients as possible, but evolutionary theory predicts that to survive pregnancy, mothers need to keep some of these nutrients for themselves.

phys.org/news/2026-11-oregon-h5n1-case-c.title: Oregon logs its first H5N1 case in cows; farmers' union says human avian flu cases underreported in Washington
phys.org/news/2026-11-oregon-h5n1-case-c.excerpt: Earlier this week, the U.S. Department of Agriculture's Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (USDA's APHIS) announced the first detection of H5N1 avian flu in a dairy herd in Oregon.

phys.org/news/2026-11-young-green-turtle.title: Young green turtles find refuge in man-made lagoon in protected UAE wetland
phys.org/news/2026-11-young-green-turtle.excerpt: A protected wetland in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has become an oasis for young sea turtles, new research shows. The study tracked nine juvenile green turtles (shell length less than 60 cm (24 inches)) and found they were "highly resident" in the Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area—spending over 80% of their time there.

phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-undp.html.title: Act now against El Niño or costs will double, UNDP warns
phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-undp.html.excerpt: Acting now to counter the devastating effects of the El Niño phenomenon will cost half as much as waiting, the head of the U.N. Development Programme told AFP Friday.

phys.org/news/2026-11-optical-multiple-i.title: Optical system maps multiple infrared fields onto one small detector
phys.org/news/2026-11-optical-multiple-i.excerpt: Researchers from the Changchun Institute of Optics, Fine Mechanics and Physics of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have developed an optical system that focuses light from several subfields onto a single small-format detector. By analyzing field-dependent spot shapes, the system identifies which subfield an isolated infrared target comes from. In sequence-level tests, it identified the correct field in about 89% of cases. The study is published in Optics and Laser Technology.

phys.org/news/2026-11-baby-corals-house-.title: Baby corals go house-hunting, gaining swimming skills as they grow
phys.org/news/2026-11-baby-corals-house-.excerpt: Coral reefs are beautiful and important, both for humans and for marine biodiversity. Corals are living creatures, although they appear to remain fixed in one place, catching small crustaceans and other tasty morsels that drift past.

phys.org/news/2026-11-climate-anxiety-yo.title: Why climate anxiety makes some youth take action, while others freeze
phys.org/news/2026-11-climate-anxiety-yo.excerpt: While young people are constantly exposed to news about climate change, their resulting anxiety does not always translate into environmental action. A new study published in Climate reveals that the relationship between climate distress and climate action is highly complex. While worry pushes some youth to seek solutions, it causes others to freeze up.

phys.org/news/2026-11-axes-coarse-potter.title: Double axes and coarse pottery reveal connections across the Rhine 5,000 years ago
phys.org/news/2026-11-axes-coarse-potter.excerpt: The Rhine, as the boundary between Western and Central Europe, appears to be a constant feature of European history. As early as the late fourth and early third millennia B.C., the traces of human activity east and west of the river differed. Archaeologists have long concluded that the river was a kind of barrier at that time, just as it has been in more recent centuries.

phys.org/news/2026-11-microscopic-solar-.title: Microscopic solar panels could help shape 3D-printed biological tissue
phys.org/news/2026-11-microscopic-solar-.excerpt: Bioprinting uses living cells and molecular signals to produce biological tissues and even whole organs, building them layer by layer in the lab. To keep the bioink, or blend of cells and materials that power this printing, correctly aligned to grow a target tissue, researchers use electricity. However, this typically requires bulky electronic interfaces and invasive wiring.

phys.org/news/2026-11-reveals-humor-succ.title: New research reveals when humor helps—and hurts—recruitment success
phys.org/news/2026-11-reveals-humor-succ.excerpt: Humor is becoming an increasingly popular feature of job advertisements, with employers using it to stand out, capture attention and attract potential candidates.

phys.org/news/2026-11-space-junk-crisis-.title: Solving the space junk crisis isn't just about counting trash—it's about control and economics
phys.org/news/2026-11-space-junk-crisis-.excerpt: If people ever think about cleaning up space debris, they typically think of something equivalent to a giant garbage truck in the sky, collecting lost astronaut tools and dead satellites, then hauling them back down to Earth to be deposited in a landfill. But dealing with space debris doesn't work that way, and a new paper by Dr. Slava Turyshev of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, available as a preprint on arXiv, makes a good argument as to why. We typically cover Turyshev for his work on the solar gravitational lens idea.

phys.org/news/2026-11-oahu-infrastructur.title: Oʻahu infrastructure threatened by tipping point in sea-level rise impacts
phys.org/news/2026-11-oahu-infrastructur.excerpt: A new comprehensive study by researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi (UH) at Mānoa Climate Resilience Collaborative reveals that traditional sea-level rise models, which account only for rising ocean waters, drastically underestimate the true threat to coastal infrastructure on Oʻahu, Hawai'i.

phys.org/news/2026-11-quarter-world-rept.title: A quarter of the world's reptiles use rocky habitats. So why aren't we protecting them?
phys.org/news/2026-11-quarter-world-rept.excerpt: Ask any reptile lover where to find a cold-blooded creature, and chances are they will point to a rocky outcrop.

phys.org/news/2026-11-concrete-steel-man.title: Concrete and steel—or mangroves and forests? When it comes to climate adaptation, nature is much cheaper
phys.org/news/2026-11-concrete-steel-man.excerpt: What's the best way to protect ourselves against climate change? The default is to reach for concrete and steel to build seawalls, dikes, dams and drainage systems. These can work. But they are expensive and inflexible. There's another, much cheaper option which gets vastly less attention. Mangroves, forests and urban trees can help protect humans and their homes, farms and cities from floods, droughts, rising seas and heat.

phys.org/news/2026-11-wider-daily-temper.title: Wider daily temperature ranges linked to stronger fevers in amphibians and reptiles
phys.org/news/2026-11-wider-daily-temper.excerpt: When amphibians and reptiles get an infection, they sometimes raise their body temperature above its usual level by moving to a warmer environment. This well-documented behavioral response is known as behavioral fever.

phys.org/news/2026-11-euclid-stone-3d-sk.title: Euclid's first data release: A stepping stone to its 3D map of the sky
phys.org/news/2026-11-euclid-stone-3d-sk.excerpt: The ESA's Euclid has already teased us with some early results. In the past, it's given us a small image covering 60 square degrees of the sky, created with a few days of observations. Those images showed individual targets from the Horsehead Nebula to the Perseus cluster of galaxies.

phys.org/news/2026-11-multidrug-resistan.title: How a multidrug-resistant bacterial clone emerged, evolved and disappeared in a hospital
phys.org/news/2026-11-multidrug-resistan.excerpt: Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium is listed by the World Health Organization as one of the highest-priority bacteria in its 2024 Bacterial Priority Pathogens List, ahead of MRSA, due to its ability to transfer resistance genes between humans, animals and the environment.

phys.org/news/2026-11-montreal-cities-co.title: Helping Montreal and other cities keep more institutional and commercial food waste out of the dump
phys.org/news/2026-11-montreal-cities-co.excerpt: Businesses and institutions in just 6% of Montreal's mapped area account for about 100,000 metric tons (110,000 tons) of food waste sent to landfill each year—half of the total amount from nonhousehold sources in the city as a whole, McGill University researchers found. Food service and retail businesses were found to be the biggest contributors.

phys.org/news/2026-11-riders-disabilitie.title: Riders with disabilities face roadblocks when finding public transportation
phys.org/news/2026-11-riders-disabilitie.excerpt: A new national database developed at the University of Michigan shows that none of the top 99 public transportation systems in the United States are easy for people with disabilities to use in four key areas of accommodation and accessibility.

phys.org/news/2026-11-career-stakes-chin.title: How career stakes shaped China's one-child policy enforcement
phys.org/news/2026-11-career-stakes-chin.excerpt: China's one-child policy is widely considered one of the most stringent public policies in modern history. Yet researchers have long debated how much it actually contributed to the country's dramatic fertility decline.

phys.org/news/2026-11-spacex-starship-sp.title: SpaceX Starship test to attempt first-ever spaceship 'catch'
phys.org/news/2026-11-spacex-starship-sp.excerpt: Elon Musk's SpaceX was poised Friday to carry out its latest test of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket, the Starship, with plans for a groundbreaking "catch" of the spaceship following a day in orbit.

phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-blame-indon.title: El Niño mostly to blame for Indonesian wildfires: Research
phys.org/news/2026-11-el-nio-blame-indon.excerpt: Wildfires that consumed vast swaths of Indonesia this year were driven largely by a strong El Niño, fueled by climate change and decades of natural landscape destruction, researchers said Friday.

phys.org/news/2026-11-molecules-porous-c.title: Light-activated molecules in porous crystals show potential for quantum chemical sensing
phys.org/news/2026-11-molecules-porous-c.excerpt: An international research team led by Nobuhiro Yanai from the University of Tokyo and Michael R. Wasielewski from Northwestern University has created polarized radical pairs, molecules with unpaired electrons whose spins align, in metal–organic frameworks (MOFs), porous materials consisting of metal ions linked by organic molecules.

phys.org/news/2026-11-couple-chromium-ru.title: A perfect couple: Chromium keeps ruthenium grounded in water electrolysis
phys.org/news/2026-11-couple-chromium-ru.excerpt: They say opposites attract, and many couples do fit this pattern. One is pragmatic and down-to-earth, while the other is a dreamer with their head in the clouds. Yet, these differences make them perfect for each other. According to researchers at ICFO, chemical interactions between atoms are not that different. Ruthenium, for instance, belongs to the "dreamer" class. It is commonly used in single-atom catalysts that speed up water electrolysis, which splits water to obtain green hydrogen. However, on its own, ruthenium tends to over-oxidize and dissolve during operation, like an idealist who takes flight without looking back.

Detecting such minute levels usually requires specialized laboratory tools and trained experts.

9.headline: Ultracold Rubidium Atoms Mimic Schwinger Pair Production
9.summary: Researchers used an optical lattice of ultracold rubidium atoms to simulate the elusive Schwinger effect, revealing how mass and field strength control pair creation.
highlights: Ultracold rubidium atoms were arranged in a one‑dimensional optical lattice to represent a false vacuum
Tuning the simulated particle mass and background electric field altered the observed pair‑production rate
Quantum gas microscope imaging captured real‑time dynamics of the simulated particle‑antiparticle creation

7.headline: Delayed Rise of Lyman Continuum Escape in Bursty High‑Redshift Galaxies
7.summary: Simulations show that Lyman continuum escape fractions peak about 16 Myr after star‑formation bursts, especially in massive early galaxies.
highlights: Typical LyC escape lag is ~16 Myr with peak correlations of 0.4‑0.6 in massive haloes
Delay scales as M★⁻⁰·¹⁹ and Mhalo⁻⁰·²⁷, lengthening for lower‑mass systems
Hα‑to‑UV luminosity ratio retains a delayed link to LyC escape, offering an observable tracer

15.headline: Astrolabe Surrogate Generates Full‑Resolution Cosmology Simulations via Flow Matching
15.summary: Astrolabe uses a flow‑matching transformer to emulate particle‑level cosmology, delivering accurate large‑scale structure without voxel resolution limits.
highlights: Acts directly on 6N phase‑space coordinates of individual particles
Employs a hybrid transformer where each particle cross‑attends to multiscale field tokens
Matches physical flow using approximate COLA coordinates, preserving momentum and mass
Reproduces power spectra, halo mass functions, velocity and density profiles in Lambda‑CDM tests
Generalizes to dark‑acoustic oscillation initial conditions and scales to TNG50‑3‑dark size

8.headline: Scientists Capture Electrons Leaping Across Forbidden Gaps in Graphene
8.summary: Using a photoemission momentum microscope, researchers observed electrons in graphene making Landau‑Zener‑Majorana transitions with up to 100 % probability under intense light.
highlights: Electrons crossed forbidden energy gaps in graphene with transition probabilities reaching 100 %
The experiment combined ultrafast laser pulses with a photoemission momentum microscope to record sub‑cycle electron dynamics
Ultra‑pure, rotated graphene samples from Forschungszentrum Jülich enabled clear observation of the quantum jumps

11.headline: JWST Spectroscopy Reveals Common Mini‑Quenched Galaxies at z > 4
11.summary: Deep 28‑hour NIRSpec/PRISM observations in the OASIS program find that suppressed, mini‑quenched and lulling galaxies constitute a sizable fraction of early low‑mass galaxies.
highlights: Three mini‑quenched galaxies with log(M/Msun)=8.3‑8.9 lie 1.2‑1.7 dex below the star‑forming main sequence
Five lulling galaxies show weak Balmer emission just above the quenching threshold
Suppressed galaxies represent 29% of the sample at z=4‑5.5, with a number density ≈1.6×10⁻³ Mpc⁻³ dex⁻¹
Photometric estimates overstate star‑formation rates, misclassifying most candidates without spectroscopy

12.headline: Stupendously Large Black Holes Ruled Out as Dark Matter Candidates
12.summary: New analysis of Planck CMB data shows that SLABs cannot account for dark matter, closing the mass window for these massive primordial black holes.
highlights: The study, published in Physical Review Letters, uses ESA's Planck satellite observations to test SLAB predictions.
Modelled SLABs would create isocurvature perturbations exceeding current CMB and BAO limits.
Results also disfavor PBH explanations for early massive galaxies seen by JWST and for pulsar‑timing‑array gravitational‑wave

6.headline: ALMA Detects Water, Methanol and Methyl Formate in HD 100546 and IRS 48 Disks
6.summary: ALMA band 5 observations reveal methanol‑rich IRS 48 with no water, while HD 100546 shows both water and methanol, yielding a comet‑like CH₃OH/H₂O ratio.
highlights: IRS 48 disk shows methanol detection but water vapor remains undetected, giving methanol‑to‑water column ratio >0.2.
HD 100546 disk contains water and methanol with CH₃OH/H₂O ≈0.02, matching the median cometary value.
Methyl formate‑to‑methanol ratio is ~0.2 in IRS 48 and ~2 in HD 100546, indicating chemical enhancement in the latter.
Non‑LTE analysis constrains optical depths and emitting regions of methanol lines in both disks.

4.headline: Chandra Reveals Kiloparsec-Scale Jet at Record-Breaking z=6.1
4.summary: Deep 360 ks Chandra observations resolve the distant AGN jet into two X‑ray components, showing a steep photon index and an 18% extended‑to‑core luminosity ratio.
highlights: Extended X‑ray emission splits into two slightly resolved components
Photon index of the jet is Γ = 2.25, steeper than the core’s Γ = 1.86
Extended‑to‑core luminosity ratio reaches 18%
Simulations suggest an AXIS‑like mission could boost photon counts by ~17×

melting_permafrost_arctic_rivers.headline: Melting Permafrost Drives Acid Rock Drainage in Arctic Rivers
melting_permafrost_arctic_rivers.summary: Long‑term monitoring shows sulphate and zinc spikes in Brooks Range streams after the unusually warm 2019 winter, linked to oxidative weathering of thawed permafrost sulfides.
highlights: Sulphate concentrations rose sharply in rivers draining the Brooks Range
Zinc levels increased concurrently, indicating mobilization of sulfide minerals
The 2019 winter warmth triggered rapid permafrost thaw and exposure of acid‑producing rocks
Similar chemical shifts have been reported in Yukon watersheds, suggesting a broader regional impact

2610_20948v1.headline: JWST Links ULX Ho II X‑1 to Highly Ionized Nebula in Holmberg II
2610_20948v1.summary: JWST IFU spectroscopy resolves a 15‑25 pc nebula around ULX Ho II X‑1, detecting [Ne V] and [Ne VI] and revealing anisotropic ionization linked to radio jets.
highlights: First detection of [Ne V] and [Ne VI] emission from the ULX nebula.
Highest‑ionization lines originate from compact regions offset toward known radio knots.
Emission lines are narrow, indicating quiescent gas and ruling out shock‑driven ionization.
Ionization extends over ~100 pc, showing the ULX’s black hole powers extreme nebular excitation.

desi_dr1_lrg2_model_independent.headline: DESI DR1 LRG2 Analysis Yields Model‑Independent Distance and Growth Measurements
desi_dr1_lrg2_model_independent.summary: Using a new emulator that varies power‑spectrum shape, DESI DR1 LRG2 data provide Alcock‑Paczynski and growth rate constraints consistent with flat ΛCDM.
highlights: Gaussian‑process emulator trained on N‑body simulation templates enables simultaneous fitting of shape, distance and growth
Measured Alcock‑Paczynski parameters α⊥ and α∥ and growth rate fσ8 differ by less than one‑twentieth of their uncertainties when
Projected onto flat ΛCDM the results give Hubble constant h = 0.724 ± 0.017 with χ² = 0.7 for two degrees of freedom

arxiv_2610_21628v1.headline: Richness Shapes Thermal Sunyaev‑Zel'dovich Signals in Galaxy Halos
arxiv_2610_21628v1.summary: A study of 7 million DESI Legacy Survey galaxies finds that thermal Sunyaev‑Zel'dovich pressure profiles vary with richness, challenging universal feedback models.
highlights: Thermal Sunyaev‑Zel'dovich Effect detected down to halo masses of 10^{12.2} M_⊙ at 5.8σ using ACT and Planck data
Mass‑richness bins show both standard GNFW profiles and flatter, mis‑centered profiles with β ranging from 1.3 to 5.49
In low‑mass, low‑richness halos the thermal energy‑mass relation deviates from self‑similarity by 7.3σ, making them key

hi_rotation_curves_568_galaxies.headline: Apertif Survey Delivers Largest HI Rotation Curve Sample of 568 Galaxies
hi_rotation_curves_568_galaxies.summary: The Apertif Wide-area Extragalactic Survey released 568 reliable HI kinematic models, providing rotation curves that span 20–300 km/s and extend up to 60 kpc.
highlights: 568 galaxies yield rotation curves with 3–23 data points each, peaking at four points.
HI disks cover three orders of magnitude in HI mass and reach radii of 2–60 kpc.
The HI mass‑size relation for 213 galaxies shows a slope of 1.96 ± 0.03 with scatter ~0.101 dex.
Intrinsic scatter of the relation is only 0.067 ± 0.007 dex, indicating nearly constant average HI surface density.

nonlocal_gravity_desi_constraints.headline: DESI Data Tighten Limits on Nonlocal Gravity Model Near ΛCDM
nonlocal_gravity_desi_constraints.summary: Recent DESI baryon acoustic oscillation measurements constrain the Maggiore‑Mancarella nonlocal R □⁻² R gravity model, showing it aligns closely with the ΛCDM paradigm.
highlights: The nonlocal parameter maps to a specific (w₀,wₐ) trajectory in the CPL plane.
Implemented the model in a Boltzmann solver and ran MCMC with CMB, supernova, and DESI BAO data.
DESI BAO results push the nonlocal parameter toward the ΛCDM limit.
No statistically significant evidence favors deviations from standard cosmology.

2610_20714v1.headline: Pristine Survey DR2 Delivers Metallicities for 15 Million Stars to G≈20.5
2610_20714v1.summary: The second data release of the Pristine survey provides photometric metallicities for 15 million FGK stars down to magnitude G≈20.5, expanding coverage to 8,000 deg².
highlights: Covers ~8,000 deg², adding 1,500 deg² since DR1.
Includes >200,000 very metal‑poor and >6,500 extremely metal‑poor star candidates.
Calibrated with Gaia DR3 synthetic CaHK photometry via the PhotCalib neural network.
Validated against DESI metallicities, showing good agreement.
Reaches faint limit G≈20.5, three magnitudes deeper than previous release.

dust_cosmic_dawn_2026_10_16.headline: ALMA2040 to Reveal Hidden Dust and Star Formation Beyond Redshift 8
dust_cosmic_dawn_2026_10_16.summary: A next‑generation sub‑millimeter array, ALMA2040, will boost sensitivity tenfold, enabling routine detection of dust emission in galaxies at z > 8 and quantifying obscured star formation.
highlights: ALMA2040 offers an order‑of‑magnitude sensitivity increase over current ALMA
Will measure dust masses, temperatures, and infrared luminosities of early galaxies
Simultaneous far‑infrared line observations will probe supernova versus grain‑growth dust production
Enables assessment of how much star formation JWST‑identified galaxies miss due to dust

2610_20730v1.headline: ALMA2040 to Reveal Birth of Star‑Forming Clumps in Early Galaxies
2610_20730v1.summary: The upcoming ALMA2040 array will resolve individual giant molecular clouds in galaxies beyond redshift 1, linking cold gas to star‑forming clumps observed by JWST and HST.
highlights: ALMA2040 will achieve sub‑mm sensitivity and angular resolution sufficient to detect GMCs at cosmological distances
CO and [CII] line imaging will map molecular gas mass, temperature, and dynamics in lensed and unlensed galaxies
Combined with JWST and ELT observations, the program will connect dust, gas, and young stars across Cosmic Noon to the Epoch of
The study will test whether clumps arise from disk instability or external disturbances, informing models of galaxy evolution

deep_sleep_muscle_fat_brain.headline: Deep Sleep Triggers Hormone Circuit That Builds Muscle and Sharpens Brain
deep_sleep_muscle_fat_brain.summary: A newly mapped hypothalamic circuit shows deep non‑REM sleep drives growth hormone release, which in turn regulates wakefulness and metabolism, researchers report.
highlights: Neurons in the hypothalamus coordinate GHRH and somatostatin activity during non‑REM and REM sleep
Growth hormone feeds back to activate locus coeruleus neurons, influencing the transition to wakefulness
The circuit was identified using implanted electrodes and optogenetic stimulation in mice
Findings were published in Cell and may guide therapies for metabolic and neurological disorders

jwst_wasp17b_atmosphere_bulge.institution: NASA / James Webb Space Telescope Team
jwst_wasp17b_atmosphere_bulge.headline: James Webb Maps Lopsided Atmosphere on Hot Jupiter WASP-17b
jwst_wasp17b_atmosphere_bulge.summary: Using JWST, astronomers discovered that the atmosphere of WASP-17b bulges on its evening side, revealing extreme winds reshape hot‑Jupiter atmospheres.
highlights: The bulge appears on the planet’s evening limb, where winds transport heat from the day‑side to the night‑side.
The discovery was made with a new ‘transmission strings’ technique that maps atmospheric thickness at different angles.
Observations were part of JWST’s TST DREAMS Guaranteed Time program and are published in Nature Astronomy.
WASP‑17b lies 1,300 light‑years away and is a classic hot Jupiter orbiting very close to its star.

exoplanet_weather_jwst.headline: Webb Telescope Uncovers Ordered Weather Patterns on Distant Brown Dwarf
exoplanet_weather_jwst.summary: Using JWST data, researchers found that the turbulent brown dwarf SIMP 0136 exhibits three recurring atmospheric states driven by temperature shifts and cloud structure.
highlights: Principal Component Analysis identified two dominant components—temperature fluctuations and vertical cloud changes—explaining
Three distinct weather states rotate into view, alternating between hotter thin‑cloud regions and cooler thick‑cloud layers.
The method offers a rapid first‑step tool for analyzing JWST observations of brown dwarfs and giant exoplanets.

brain_cells_cognitive_decline.headline: Dysfunctional Oligodendrocytes Linked to Age‑Related Cognitive Decline
brain_cells_cognitive_decline.summary: Scientists found that aging oligodendrocytes produce abnormal myelin, damaging nerve fibers and accelerating memory and thinking decline in older adults.
highlights: Abnormal myelin buildup and loss of large nerve fibers were observed in brains of participants with faster cognitive decline
Reduced NRF2 protein in oligodendrocytes caused excess myelin and impaired learning in mouse models
Drugs that activate the NRF2 pathway are already used for multiple sclerosis, suggesting a repurposing opportunity

necklace_atoms.headline: Physicists Freeze Atomic 'Necklaces' to Reveal Century‑Old Bethe Strings
necklace_atoms.summary: Using ultracold cesium atoms in one‑dimensional tubes, researchers observed Bethe string clusters, confirming a quantum prediction made by Hans Bethe nearly a century ago.
